paper_metadata.title: Quantum algorithm for credit valuation adjustments

summary: The paper proposes a gate‑based quantum algorithm for computing credit valuation adjustment (CVA) using amplitude estimation with engineered likelihood functions. For a benchmark European option instance, the authors estimate that achieving 0.001% relative error would take ~4.9×10^5 seconds on a fault‑tolerant quantum computer (13 logical qubits, surface code assumptions) versus ~3.7×10^6 seconds for classical Monte Carlo, though classical methods remain faster for typical accuracy regimes and the results are based entirely on simulation and resource modeling.

experiments.description: Noiseless gate-based quantum CVA evaluation using a hybrid circuit with state preparation (QCBM or MPS) and controlled rotations (CRCA or RLS), followed by amplitude estimation via engineered likelihood functions.

algorithm.variant: Engineered likelihood function (ELF) amplitude estimation for CVA; state preparation via QCBM or MPS; controlled rotations via CRCA
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Training until target KL divergence / cost convergence; amplitude estimation performed with ELF iterations until desired statistical precision

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Time encoded in m qubits and asset price encoded in n qubits; joint distribution over discretized (time, price) grid loaded into amplitudes. Ancilla qubits used for payoff, default probability, and discount factor.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate CVA = (1-R) * E_q(t)[p(t) E_P(s|t)[v(s,t)]] = (1-R) ∫ q(t)p(t)∫P(s|t)v(s,t)dsdt, reduced to estimating ⟨ξ|Π|ξ⟩ for the discretized bracketed term in Eq. (7).
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Amplitude estimation with projector onto ancilla state |111⟩; no explicit optimization constraints beyond circuit training

problem_instance.description: Single-asset European call CVA benchmark instance with discretized time and price; benchmarked against Monte Carlo and exact circuit simulation.

dataset_specification.asset_price_paths: 10^5 Monte Carlo trajectories for benchmark distribution learning
dataset_specification.price_grid: N=2^n with n=2 for the main instance

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Monte Carlo simulation of geometric Brownian motion; price range chosen as [max(μ̂-3σ̂,0), μ̂+3σ̂]; price data binned to discrete sj values; default probabilities bootstrapped from CDS spreads; EONIA curve used for discounting.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Exact simulation of the trained quantum circuit; comparison to Monte Carlo benchmark CVAMC and discretized benchmark CVA(2); error decomposition into discretization, circuit, and observable errors

implementation_details.classical_solver: Monte Carlo simulation in Orquestra integration with quantlib
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical Monte Carlo generation of target distribution for QCBM/MPS training; bootstrapping hazard rates from CDS spreads
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: CVA computed from sampled expectation values and error decomposition

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Training curves shown for QCBM/MPS/CRCA; exact iteration counts reported for some subroutines in tables

speedup_claims.conditions: amplitude estimation in the ideal low-noise regime; statistical error dominates
speedup_claims.caveats: Quantum advantage is limited by circuit depth, state-preparation error, and fault-tolerant overhead; paper notes practical advantage only at very small target error.

speedup_claims.conditions: assumed all-to-all connectivity, physical gate error rate 1e-3, surface code distance 18, 1 µs cycle time
speedup_claims.caveats: Projection depends strongly on hardware assumptions and exact implementation details.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/ε_S) for amplitude estimation; state preparation and controlled rotation circuits are designed to reduce depth relative to reversible logic synthesis
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/ε_S^2) Monte Carlo sampling for statistical error; additional discretization overhead for time/price grids
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Relative error ≲ 0.0067% in the paper's resource model
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: 4.9×10^5 s at relative error 0.001% under assumed fault-tolerant hardware
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: 3.7×10^6 s on single-core classical computer for the same instance

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Relative error ≤ ~0.0067% according to the authors’ runtime model
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant device with surface code distance ≈18, ~13 logical qubits, logical two‑qubit gate error rates derived from physical error rate 10^-3, and long runtime (~10^5–10^6 seconds)
limiting_factors: Only quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation
Large overhead from quantum error correction
Complex state preparation and controlled‑rotation circuits
Advantage appears only for extremely small statistical error targets

notes: num_qubits=7 inferred from 2 time qubits + 2 price qubits + 3 ancilla qubits; the paper explicitly states a total of 7 qubits for the CVA instance in the RLS discussion and 13 logical qubits for the ELF sampling circuit in the resource-estimation section, but the main noiseless CVA circuit uses 7 qubits.
hardware.type inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper reports an exact simulation of the quantum circuit for the noiseless CVA value and does not name a physical QPU for this experiment.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported for the noiseless CVA circuit; only gate counts and resource estimates for subroutines are given.
Authors present a projected runtime comparison and discuss potential advantage at very high accuracy but do not demonstrate it experimentally.
Classical Monte Carlo remains faster for practical error regimes in their simulations.
